episode_title: Restoring Respect & Rebuilding the Future of the Trades

real_qa.q: What is the gender pay gap in non-union construction compared to union scale positions?
real_qa.r: In the non-union sector, women earn approximately 84 cents on the dollar compared to men who get paid considerably more. In contrast, union positions operate on standardized scales: first-year apprentices earn about 60% to 65% of the journeyman scale, then progress year by year to the full journeyman rate. However, women in management roles like project managers, field engineers, and project superintendents still do not receive equal pay for the same work as their male counterparts, even in union environments.
real_qa.requete: gender pay gap construction union non-union

real_qa.q: What are the entry-level wage expectations for apprentices in construction trades?
real_qa.r: A first-year apprentice in union trades typically earns 60% to 65% of the journeyman scale, which these days is a pretty good wage to earn per hour. Journeyman wages nowadays, factoring in a little overtime, can easily reach $80,000 to $100,000 a year, plus benefits including an annuity or 401k and sometimes a vacation fund.

real_qa.q: Why do women perform better at welding jobs in the construction trades according to job site observations?
real_qa.r: Women tend to be more meticulous and know how to slow down and do the job carefully, making them skilled welders. Even men on job sites acknowledge this, saying women are just better welders because they take their time, whereas men often want to get in there, get it done, and move on to the next one. This applies across harder trades like boilermakers, ironworkers, and pipe fitters.
real_qa.requete: why women better welders construction trades

real_qa.q: What role did the removal of shop classes from high school curriculum play in the construction workforce pipeline?
real_qa.r: High schools used to offer metalworking, architectural drafting, shop class, woodworking, and automotive classes. Teachers could identify kids with real skills for mechanics or drafting. The removal of these classes has been devastating for youth because guidance counselors continue pushing college exclusively, even though college is not for everybody and the trades offer viable career paths.
real_qa.requete: shop class removed high school construction vocational

real_qa.q: What strategies should construction company leaders use to recruit and retain women in the field?
real_qa.r: Construction company leaders should attend career fairs with booths and hands-on presentations showing what they do and what kind of people they look for. Smaller contractors doing well with retention should recruit kids on Saturdays to show them exactly what they do. Companies should also partner with programs like Habitat for Humanity to let families get hands-on experience. Executive presence at career days, showing kids real work environments safely, helps demystify construction and builds interest from a young age.
real_qa.requete: construction company recruit retain women workforce

real_qa.q: How does the construction trade pathway provide economic security for single parent families compared to other careers?
real_qa.r: Single-parent women are highly encouraged to enter the trades because they will earn a living wage even as apprentices, and they receive insurance which makes a big difference in reducing financial burden. However, disparate equal opportunity persists when employers assume mothers will take days off if a child gets sick, creating workplace bias that is hard to overcome despite women having jobs too.
real_qa.requete: single parent women construction trades living wage

guest.bio_context: Kim Pierce grew up in Northern Minnesota where her father was a carpenter with his own business. She spent 34+ years in the trades, initially obtaining an accounting diploma from a two-year vocational school before returning to construction. She became President and CEO of her family's construction business and held a general contractor's license from the state of Minnesota in 1994, one of only two or three women in her licensing class. After disbanding the family business, she joined the union as a laborer, spent 10 years with the ironworkers union traveling across the U.S., then returned to school in her mid-30s, graduating in 2008 with a construction safety certification, and has held her current position as a construction safety professional ever since.
